tagline.text: A canyon-edge drive up to Baguio, opened in 1905

location.label: Location
location.text: Tuba, Benguet to Rosario, La Union (the road into Baguio)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–April dry season (closures are frequent in the rainy and typhoon season)

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: Half a day round trip (about 1 hour one way, 2–3 hours with stops)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300~1,500 (per person, day trip; excludes car rental, fuel and tolls; rough estimate)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Clark International Airport (CRK) or Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL), then overland

children.text: Kennon Road is a road of about 33.5km that climbs along canyon cliffs from Rosario, La Union to Baguio, opened on January 29, 1905 during the American colonial period. The canyon scenery, the Lion's Head monument and the zigzag section are the highlights, but rockfalls and closures are frequent, so checking the latest advisory before you leave is essential.
Kennon Road is a two-lane road linking Baguio City in Benguet and Rosario in La Union, also called the Rosario–Baguio Road. It is about

long and part of National Route N54, and most of it runs through the municipality of Tuba, Benguet. The Bued River flows through a rocky canyon along the road, and the road is cut into the canyon wall above it. An experienced driver in a car is said to need about 45 minutes to 1 hour for the climb. The road's kilometer posts count from Rizal Park in Manila as zero, and the southern end at the Rosario junction is at about
, while the northern end at the Baguio roundabout is at about
. At that roundabout Governor Pack Road and the Aspiras–Palispis Highway meet, and a little further on the road splits into Loakan Road and Monticello Road.
The road was built because the American colonial government wanted a reliable route to develop Baguio as a summer capital. Construction began in
and the road opened on
January 29, 1905

. It is named for Colonel Lyman Kennon of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and it was originally called Benguet Road. The colonial government spent more than US$2.7 million, and the project was regarded as one of the most difficult and expensive civil engineering works of its time.

More than 2,300 workers from 36 countries took part in the construction, and Japanese workers are said to have been the largest foreign group. Hundreds died of malaria and dysentery, and some fell to their deaths from the cliffs. Some of the workers from Hong Kong and Japan stayed on in Baguio after the road was finished. The Camps 1 to 8 set up along the way were housing for the workers, and are now villages where local residents live (Camps 1–8).

The road is still counted among the most dangerous in the Philippines, with many accidents in the rainy season. It was severely damaged in the July 1990 Luzon earthquake and permanent closure was discussed for a time, but it reopened on September 1, 1991 after rehabilitation. It has been closed often in recent years by heavy rain, rockfalls and repair work, and in December 2021 Republic Act No. 11604 made full rehabilitation and maintenance a government obligation. So the drive itself is the attraction, but you must first check whether the road is open that day. The government has also been considering a public-private partnership to improve the road.
The road follows the upper wall of the rocky canyon cut by the Bued River. In each stretch that opens toward the canyon you can see the deep gorge below and the mountain slope opposite.

The stretch between Camp 6 and Camp 7 is the steepest and most winding part of the road. With one sharp bend after another, you must slow down and watch the oncoming lane. The Camp 6 area has many rockfalls and is where the rock shed was installed, so be sure to follow road signs and the instructions of traffic enforcers while driving.
A lion-shaped monument on the boundary between Tuba and Baguio, it is the symbol of Kennon Road. The upper tollgate is said to be near it, at Camp 6.
A waterfall that is described as visible from Kennon Road on the Bued River canyon side. After rain the flow swells and it is easier to see.

The camps where the construction workers stayed are now roadside villages. Near Camp 1 are a bridge over the Bued River and the junction with the Kennon–Agat Road. Each numbered camp has its own village feel, and as you drive through you can see small shops and roadside stalls.

blocks.title: A steep climb from Rosario to Baguio

children.text: Starting from Rosario near the coast, you gain a great deal of elevation over about 33km up to the highland city of Baguio. As you near Baguio, you notice the change as pine trees and cooler air begin.
To block falling rocks, a rock shed 152 meters long was built in the Camp 6 section. Its cost was reported at about ₱264 million, and the road was closed for about two months during installation.

blocks.title: A road from the American era

children.text: It was first built by laying and packing stone, then changed to asphalt, and some parts have been replaced with concrete. It has great historical meaning as a road marked by American colonial engineering and the sacrifice of many workers. The retaining wall at the Uabac section was damaged by heavy rain and its rehabilitation was completed in 2016.
Before leaving, check the road's open status and vehicle restrictions with the DPWH Cordillera office and local news. If it is closed, switch to Marcos Highway or Naguilian Road.
Enter the road at Rosario and pass the lower tollgate near Camp 1.
Where there is a safe shoulder in the canyon section, stop briefly to see the view. Do not stand for long in rockfall zones.
Climb the Camp 6–7 zigzag section slowly and check the condition of the rock shed entrance.
Take photos near Lion's Head, pass the upper tollgate and enter Baguio.
Once in Baguio, have lunch at Burnham Park or Session Road and continue your city itinerary.
An experienced driver in a car can take about 45 minutes to 1 hour, but allow a generous 2–3 hours including stops and traffic.

items.title: Coming down from Baguio
items.subtitle: Downhill driving and a coastal evening

children.text: Finish your city itinerary in Baguio, check again whether Kennon Road is open, and head down.
Drive down slowly using engine braking at Lion's Head and the zigzag section.
Pass Camp 1 and the lower tollgate and come out at Rosario.
Head to the La Union coast and enjoy the sunset and dinner in San Juan or San Fernando.
After dark the canyon section is very dangerous, so pass through it before sunset.

From Manila, take NLEX, SCTEX and TPLEX north, exit near Rosario to N2 (MacArthur Highway), and enter Kennon Road. Check distances and tolls for each section on a map app and in expressway advisories.
The southern end of Kennon Road is the Rosario junction with N2, and the northern end is the roundabout in Baguio.
Kennon Road is a toll road, with fees collected at a lower and an upper tollgate. Fees can change, so confirm locally.
Buses and vans to Baguio use Kennon Road, Marcos Highway or Naguilian Road depending on the route and weather. Confirm which road they take before boarding.
Large buses and trucks are often restricted and sometimes detour by another road.
From Clark International Airport (CRK) you can go north on TPLEX toward Rosario. Flights change by season, so check airline announcements.
Marcos Highway, Naguilian Road and the Asin–Nangalisan–San Pascual–La Union boundary road are advised as alternate routes. Use them when Kennon Road is closed or restricted.

Kennon Road is relatively safest in the dry season from November to April. In the rainy and typhoon season, heavy rain raises the risk of rockfalls and landslides, so closures are frequent. Setting out on a clear morning gives the sharpest view of the canyon.
After rain the waterfalls swell, but the risk of rockfalls and road subsidence rises too. If a typhoon is forecast, postpone your trip.

There is almost no lodging on Kennon Road itself, only roadside stalls and small shops. There are many places to stay and eat in Baguio and on the La Union coast (San Juan, San Fernando), so it is common to go up and down in a day trip and stay in one of those places.

In Baguio, vegetables, strawberries and highland coffee are well known, and the La Union coast is good for seafood. Restaurants open, close and move, so check ratings and opening status before you go.
Before leaving, check the DPWH Cordillera office's announcements and local news for open status and vehicle restrictions. Even in 2025–2026 the road opened and closed several times.
A March 2026 report said that only light vehicles up to 5 tons could pass, while large buses and trucks were restricted. This may have changed again since.

The temporary Acrow bridge at Camp 2 was announced with a vertical clearance of about 2.5 meters, and the rock shed entrance has at times narrowed to one lane. Check ahead if you have a large vehicle.
If you are inexperienced, climb and descend the zigzag section slowly in a low gear. Use engine braking on the downhill.
Plan your trip to pass through before sunset. Fog and darkness make the canyon section much more dangerous.
Stop only on safe shoulders, and do not stand for long in rockfall zones.
Some stretches may have weak phone signal, so download an offline map.
Follow the instructions of the police or road officers and the one-lane traffic signals.
If Kennon Road is closed when you are in Baguio, come down by Marcos Highway or Naguilian Road. A September 2026 report said both were passable.

Kennon Road has a risk of rockfalls and landslides. A September 2026 report said that at times non-residents were restricted and only one lane was allowed at Camp 6, so be sure to check that it is open today.
In May 2026 a retaining wall collapsed and all vehicles were blocked for a time, and restrictions changed repeatedly afterward. Check the latest advisory.
Road subsidence (for example around Camp 3, Tuba) and rockfalls can occur, so it is safer to avoid the road in the rainy season.
Heavy rain and typhoons close the road because of landslide risk, so check the weather forecast first.
With sharp bends one after another on a narrow two-lane road, avoid overtaking and speeding, and avoid driving at night.
Tollgates and vehicle restrictions can change, so carry cash and small change.
Travel time varies greatly with weather and closures, so leave plenty of margin on days when you have a flight or bus connection in La Union or Baguio.
The highland city at the northern end of Kennon Road, with Burnham Park, Session Road and Camp John Hay.
A lake park in downtown Baguio, a good place to rest after arriving by Kennon Road.
After coming down toward Rosario, go north along the coastal highway to reach the surf town of San Juan.
The capital of La Union, with attractions such as Ma-Cho Temple, and a good place to finish after a Kennon Road trip.
